summary: Ages 5-6 (Y1) language/notation goal: read, write and interpret the symbols +, − and = in number sentences, attaching formal notation to the already-understood actions of combining and taking away. The central design move is to introduce = relationally ('is the same as') from the very start, presenting it in varied positions (5 = 3 + 2, 3 + 2 = 2 + 3) to pre-empt the common 'the answer comes next' operator misconception. Activities below span a hands-on sentence-builder with a balance, symbol-and-action reference work, notation practice, and a short probing dialogue — each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.
misconceptions: Reading = as 'the answer comes next' (an operator/'makes') rather than 'is the same as', so 5 = 3 + 2 or 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 look wrong.
Confusing + and − by shape/name, especially when reading quickly, or ignoring the symbol and just combining whatever numbers appear.
Writing sentences with the operation and answer in the wrong order, or omitting the = sign.
Treating the number sentence as a left-to-right instruction to 'do something' with no sense that it states a relationship.
Believing something must always be written after the = (rejecting 7 = 3 + 4 or missing-number forms).

activities.title: Sentence builder linked to a balance
steps: Push two groups of counters together on a work surface and record what happened with a sentence strip, placing a '+' between the groups; take some counters away and use a '−' instead.

Build the sentence 3 + 2 = 5 and check the two sides balance (a two-pan balance loaded with identical counters or cubes, so that weight goes up with count, or a balance image/animation that only levels when both sides have the same value).
Now build 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 and notice the sides STILL balance — discuss why this is allowed even though no single 'answer' sits after the =.
Try true/false sentences (e.g. 5 = 3 + 2 (true), 4 + 1 = 3 + 2 (true, both equal 5), 3 + 2 = 2 + 1 (false)) and predict whether the balance will level or tip before testing.
Keep the referent objects (counters / ten-frame / part-whole model) visible beside the sentence throughout.
activities.insight: The symbols record actions the child already does (+ = combining, − = taking away) and = means 'the same value on both sides', not 'write the answer here' — so numbers may legitimately appear on either side.

activities.title: Both directions: read-and-act, then write-to-match
steps: Read a symbolic sentence aloud in full mathematical language ('three plus two equals five'; 'five minus two is the same as three') and act it out with objects.
Point to each symbol in turn and say what it records: + 'put together', − 'take away', = 'is the same as'.
Watch or hear a concrete/pictorial situation (e.g. three ducks swimming and two more joining) and WRITE a number sentence that matches it, including the = sign.
Write a take-away story of your own and record it with a sentence using the − sign.
activities.insight: Reading a sentence and enacting it, and writing a sentence to capture a real situation, are two sides of the same skill: notation and spoken vocabulary co-develop and stay tied to meaning.

activities.title: Symbol-and-action reference wall
steps: Study a reference display showing each symbol beside the action it records, with a lift-the-flap or tap-to-reveal meaning ('plus means put together', 'minus means take away', 'equals means is the same as').
Study one fully worked sentence tied to a concrete model.
Use the wall as a check: when unsure which symbol to write, find the matching action.
activities.insight: A stable anchor linking each symbol to its meaning and vocabulary supports recall while building and writing sentences.

activities.title: Notation practice: choose and judge
steps: Choose the symbol that matches a described action (which sign for 'putting together'? for 'taking away'?).
Match a number sentence to the picture or story it describes.
Judge true/false for = sentences in non-standard positions: 5 = 3 + 2 (true), 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 (true), 4 + 1 = 2 + 2 (false).
activities.insight: Fluent recognition of what each symbol records, and relational judgement of = sentences, consolidates the notation and surfaces the operator-equals error.

activities.title: What does this = mean here? (short probe)
steps: Look at a true/false sentence with = in a non-standard position (e.g. 7 = 3 + 4) and explain what the = sign is telling us about the two sides.
Answer: is 5 = 3 + 2 allowed, or must it be 3 + 2 = 5? Say why.
Point to the part of a number sentence that shows a change (e.g. in 3 + 2 = 5 for the duck story, the '+ 2' shows the two more ducks arriving).
activities.insight: Articulating the relational meaning of = makes the child's reading explicit and can expose any residual operator view.

checkQuestion: Read this out loud and tell me what is happening: 3 + 2 = 5. Now here is a story — three ducks are swimming and two more come to join them. Say a number sentence for the story, and tell me what the = sign means here.
checkAnswer: Reads 'three plus two equals five'; offers 3 + 2 = 5 (or 5 = 3 + 2) for the ducks; reads = as 'is the same as' / 'makes' / 'is equal to' — not merely 'the answer is'.
